Opponent State Inference Under Partial Observability:
An HMM–POMDP Framework for 2026 Formula 1
Energy Strategy
Kalliopi Kleisarchaki
Independent Researcher
v1 (1 March 2026): Submitted to arXiv. Five observables, 30 hidden states.
v1.5 (5 March 2026): Sixth observableδ throttle added. ResearchGate pre-registration before Melbourne
(https://www.researchgate.net/publication/401621952).
v2 (post-Melbourne 8 March 2026; arXiv 9 March 2026): 40-state architecture.L harvest/Lderate split
formalised. Pre-registered on ResearchGate before China (Race 2).

Abstract
The 2026 Formula 1 technical regulations introduce a fundamental change to energy
strategy: under a 50/50 internal combustion engine / battery power split with unlimited
regeneration and a driver-controlled Override Mode (hereaftermom), the optimal energy
deployment policy depends not only on a driver’s own state but on thehidden stateof
rival cars. This creates a Partially Observable Stochastic Game that cannot be solved by
single-agent optimisation methods.
We present a tractable two-layer inference and decision framework. The first layer is a
40-stateHidden Markov Model (hmm) that infers a probability distribution over each rival’s
erscharge level—now decomposed into four modes ( H, M, Lharvest, Lderate)—Override
Mode status, and tyre degradation state from six publicly observable telemetry signals. The
second layer is a Deep Q-Network (dqn) policy that takes thehmmbelief state as input and
selects between energy deployment strategies. We formally characterise thecounter-harvest
trap—a deceptive strategy in which a car deliberately suppresses observable deployment
signals to induce a rival into a failed attack—and show that detecting it requires belief-state
inference overbothERS level and the harvest/derate sub-mode.
The Lharvest/Lderate split is the central architectural advance of v2: both sub-modes
produce depressed ∆ vtrap and can co-occur with zaero = 1 in an activation zone, but they
carryoppositestrategic implications. Lharvest means the rival is building a hidden reserve—
the trap condition. Lderate means the rival is at their physical limit—a genuine attack
opportunity. The sixth observableδ throttle (super-clipping duration fraction, added in v1.5)
provides clean separation between these sub-modes; v2 elevates this separation to thestate
levelrather than handling it as a mixed emission.
On synthetic races generated under the 40-state parametric model, thehmmachieves
96.8%ERS-level accuracy (random baseline: 25%), correctly classifies Lharvest vs. Lderate
with89.4%accuracy (random baseline: 50%), and detects counter-harvest trap conditions
with96.3%recall. Pre-season analysis indicates circuit-dependent recharge availability
(1.0× to 2.2× per lap) as the primary confound for trap detection; Melbourne represents the
hardest-case validation environment. Baum-Welch calibration on 2026 race telemetry begins
with the Australian Grand Prix (8 March 2026). Code will be made publicly available upon
acceptance.
arXiv:2603.01290v3  [cs.AI]  15 May 2026
1 Introduction
Formula 1 has always been a game of imperfect information. A driver knows their own tyre
temperature, fuel load, and energy reserves exactly; they observe rival positions through timing
screens and team radio; but theinternal stateof a rival’s car—how much battery charge they
carry, whether their Override Mode is available or spent, how degraded their tyres are—remains
hidden. For most of F1’s history this did not matter strategically: energy deployment was
constrained enough that the optimal decision could be computed from own-car state alone.
The 2026 regulations change this [FIA, 2026]. The 50/50 power split between internal
combustion engine and MGU-K battery places the battery under permanent demand, making
erscharge level a first-order strategic variable every sector. Override Mode is a proximity-gated
energy award: when a driver is within one second of the car ahead at the designated detection
point, they earn an extra 0.5 MJ of deployable energy on the following lap. Active Aero replaces
DRS entirely: the adjustable rear wing is removed and replaced with a driver-controlled binary
aero system available only in designated activation zones. Crucially, a car can run Active Aero
in straight-line modewhile harvesting—the mechanical downforce reduction provides speed
independent of battery deployment. This is the physical basis for the counter-harvest trap
(Section 3.3).
The optimal burn-or-harvest decision in any sector is now a function of thejoint stateof
both cars, not just one’s own.
Contributions
This paper makes three contributions:
1. Problem formalisation.We formally model 2026 F1 energy management as a Partially
Observable Stochastic Game (posg) and define a tractablepomdpapproximation for
the single-agent case. We precisely characterise the counter-harvest trap as a deceptive
equilibrium strategy.
2. Rival state inference.We propose a40-statehmmover rivalerscharge level (four
modes: H, M, Lharvest, Lderate), Override Mode status, and tyre degradation, initialised
from an analytically-derived emission matrix and calibrated via Baum-Welch EM on 2026
race telemetry. The Lharvest/Lderate decomposition is the architectural advance over v1.5:
it eliminates the ambiguity that v1.5 handled only at the emission level via a mixed prior.
3. Decision policy.We propose and fully specify adqnpolicy that consumes thehmm
belief state alongside own-car context features (full input specification in Appendix C),
and characterise its advantages over observable-only threshold baselines.
Scope and limitations
This paper treats rivals as stationary processes—their policies do not adapt to our inference. This
assumption is violated when rivals reason about being observed, leading to the counter-harvest
trap and non-stationary equilibria studied in Kleisarchaki [2026b]. We state this limitation at
the outset because it is not a defect to be hidden: it is precisely the gap between this paper and
its game-theoretic extension. Thepomdpsolution presented here is the correct baseline against
which that extension must demonstrate improvement.
2 Background
Prior computational work on F1 strategy has focused on pit-stop timing as an optimisation
problem [Heilmeier et al., 2020] and on reinforcement learning for race simulation [Betz et al.,
2
2022]. These formulations treat energy management as a deterministic sub-problem with known
rival actions.
The closest structural analogue to the counter-harvest trap in prior work is the Formula E
Attack Mode [Liu et al., 2021]: teams earn a temporary power boost by driving through a
designated off-line zone. The key difference is that Attack Mode is opt-in from a fixed physical
location, publicly visible to all teams, and does not interact with a rival’s inference model. The
2026 Active Aero system creates a strictly harder version: the equivalent of Attack Mode can
be executed covertly at any activation zone, at a time of the driver’s choosing, in a way that
mimics harvesting to an observer without a belief-state model.
POMDPs and opponent modelling.POMDPs [Kaelbling et al., 1998] provide the natural
framework for sequential decision-making under state uncertainty. Opponent modelling in
multi-agent systems has been approached through Bayesian inference [Albrecht and Stone,
2018], recursive reasoning [Gmytrasiewicz and Doshi, 2005], and game-theoretic agent modelling
[Hansen et al., 2004]. Our approach is closest to thehmmopponent modelling literature, where
a rival’s latent strategy or resource state is inferred from observable actions [Albrecht and Stone,
2018].
HMMs for temporal inference.HMMs [Rabiner, 1989] are well-suited to the F1 energy
inference problem: the hidden state evolves according to known physics (the transition model),
and we observe noisy projections of it each sector (the emission model). The Baum-Welch
algorithm [Baum et al., 1970] provides maximum-likelihood parameter estimation from unlabelled
sequences—critical here because we have no ground-truth labels for rival battery states in real
telemetry.
Why discrete HMM over particle filter.A particle filter could in principle handle
continuouserscharge and relax the conditional independence assumption. We use a discrete
hmmfor two reasons. First, Baum-Welch provides closed-form maximum-likelihood parameter
estimation from unlabelled sequences; particle filters require approximate inference schemes (e.g.
SMC-EM) that are substantially less stable at the small data volumes available from a single race
weekend. Second, the four-binersdiscretisation is physically motivated: the strategic decision
is whether a rivalcandefend ( ers≥M ),cannotdefend ( Lderate: physically depleted), or is
building a trap( Lharvest: deliberately conserving); a continuous representation would require
decision boundaries to be learned from data rather than specified from domain knowledge.
HMM identifiability.With 40 states and six observables discretised to 8 × 7 × 5 × 5 × 2 × 6 =
16,800 joint bins, the raw emission matrix has 40×16,800 = 672,000 parameters. With parameter
tying by (ERS, tyre) cluster (Section 4) reducing to 20 effective emission rows, and exploiting
the conditional independence structure, the effective degrees of freedom per emission row are
8+7+5+5+2+6−5 = 28, giving 20 × 28 = 560 effective parameters. The cumulative observation
count reaches ∼13,920 by Race 4. The model should be treated as empirically validated only
from Race 4 onwards; Melbourne results are explicitly preliminary.
Deep Q-Networks.DQN [Mnih et al., 2015] with Double DQN [van Hasselt et al., 2016]
and experience replay [Lin, 1992] provides the policy learning component. We use a deliberately
shallow network (three hidden layers, 256–256–128 units) because the belief state does the
representational heavy lifting and the training data volume is limited.
3
3 Problem Formalisation
3.1 The 2026 Regulatory Context
The 2026 regulations introduce three strategically relevant changes [FIA, 2026].
50/50 power split.Total power output is split equally between ICE and MGU-K battery.
The battery is under continuous demand, makingerscharge level a first-order strategic variable
at every sector.
Override Mode.A proximity-gated energy award replacing DRS entirely. When a driver is
within one second of the car ahead at the lap’s detection point (nominally the final corner), they
earn an extra 0.5 MJ of deployable energy on the following lap. When deployed, Override Mode
produces a distinctive speed signature detectable in speed-trap telemetry.
Active Aero.Replaces DRS entirely. Driver-controlled, available only in designated activation
zones, with two fixed positions (cornering and straight-line). Straight-line mode produces a speed
boost detectable as a positive ∆ vtrap increment above theers-explained baseline. Crucially, a
car can run Active Aero in straight-line mode while super-clipping ( Lderate)—the mechanical
downforce reduction provides speed independent of battery deployment. This is the physical
basis for the counter-harvest trap.
Circuit-dependent recharge shortfall.Pre-season analysis reveals recharge-per-lap ratios
from 1.0× (Australia, Italy, Saudi Arabia) to 2.2× (Azerbaijan, Singapore).1 At Melbourne, cars
require approximately 16 additional seconds of super-clipping per lap at 250 kW, transforming
super-clipping from a discretionary tool into a near-mandatory operating mode.
3.2 The POMDP Model
We model the decision problem for a single ego car as apomdp⟨S, A, T, R,Ω, O, γ⟩where:
Definition 1(Fully Observable State).The fully observable component so
t includes tyre
compound and age (FIA-published), lap number, sector, circuit position (activation zone or not),
and own-carerslevel, Override Mode status, Active Aero position, and gap to adjacent cars.
Definition 2(Hidden Rival State).The hidden state for each rival is xt = (e, m, τ) ∈ X , where:
e∈ {H, M, L harvest, L derate}(erscharge level, 4 modes) (1)
m∈ {available,spent}(Override Mode status) (2)
τ∈ {new,light,moderate,heavy,cliff}(tyre degradation) (3)
giving|X |= 4×2×5 =40states.
The Lharvest / Lderate decomposition.This is the central architectural advance of v2 over
v1.5. Both sub-modes produce depressed ∆ vtrap and may co-occur with zaero = 1 in an activation
zone, but they haveoppositestrategic implications:
•L harvest: the driver isactively managingthrottle below 100%, building a hidden energy
reserve. This is the trap condition. δthrottle ≈ 0.05–0.10 (low; managed throttle, not full
demand).
1These engineering estimates are community-derived from pre-season analysis (February 2026) and are not
FIA-certified. All downstream claims should be treated as provisional until confirmed by Race 1 telemetry.
4
•L derate: the driver demands full power ( ≥98% throttle) but the MGU-K battery has
reached its SOC ceiling and cannot deliver further electrical output. The car slows not by
choice but by physics. δthrottle ≈ 0.40–0.60 (high; full throttle with below-baseline speed).
In v1.5, both sub-modes shared the L state, and the δthrottle observable was handled as a
mixed emission with a circuit-dependent prior ( µ = 0.40 for Melbourne at recharge ratio 1.0).
This worked, but produced an ambiguous posterior over L: thehmmcould not separately report
P (Lharvest) and P (Lderate), which are the quantities thedqnpolicy actually needs. In v2, the
posterior directly provides both quantities as separate belief dimensions.
Fuel exclusion.Fuel load is excluded from the hidden state for two independent reasons:
(i) all cars start with the same regulated load and deplete it at approximately the same rate,
making fuel state deterministic from the observable lap number; and (ii) all six observables
are measured as deviations from a per-driver rolling 5-lap baseline, which absorbs the smooth
monotone pace improvement from fuel burn.
Definition 3(Action Space).A={burn,harvest}.
Definition 4(Observation Space). ot = (∆ vtrap, ∆tsector, ∆bbrake, σ2
speed, zaero, δthrottle) ∈ Ω,
where each component is a deviation from the rival’s rolling 5-lap baseline, except zaero ∈ {0, 1}
andδ throttle ∈[0,1].
The six observables are: (i) ∆ vtrap: speed at the speed trap minus rival baseline (km/h);
(ii) ∆ tsector: sector time minus rival baseline (seconds); (iii) ∆ bbrake: distance from apex at
which braking begins, minus rival baseline (metres); (iv) σ2
speed: detrended variance of rival’s
speed trace within the sector; (v) zaero ∈ {0, 1}: Active Aero deployment in straight-line mode
(observable in activation zones from speed signature); (vi) δthrottle ∈ [0, 1]: fraction of straight-line
telemetry samples within the sector where throttle ≥ 98% and speed is simultaneously below
the driver’s 5-lap rolling baseline—the mechanical signature ofersderating, added in v1.5 and
now elevated to full state-level discriminator in v2.
Definition 5(Belief State). bt ∈ ∆40 is the probability vector over hidden states, maintained
by thehmmforward algorithm:
bt(x) =P(x t =x|o 1:t) (4)
Definition 6(Reward).

3.3 The Counter-Harvest Trap
Definition 7(Counter-Harvest Trap).A deceptive strategy for a car ahead (Car B) against a
following car (Car A) in which Car B simultaneously: (i) runsersin Lharvest mode (conserving
charge deliberately); (ii) deploys Active Aero in straight-line mode within an activation zone
(maintaining straight-line speed despite harvesting); and (iii) allows the observable telemetry
signals to indicate harvesting. Car A’s inference model identifies the L-state signature as an
attack opportunity and burns energy. Car B then activates full deployment (including Override
Mode), defending the position easily because it has the full energy reserve that Car A just spent.
The trigger signature exploits a key 2026 regulatory asymmetry: lift-and-coast disables
Active Aero, but super-clipping does not. Super-clipping is the automated redirection of ICE
power to the battery at full throttle; the car slows slightly (power diverted from rear wheels)
but Active Aero remains deployed.
5
Why v2 resolves the trap ambiguity more cleanly than v1.5.In v1.5, Lharvest and
Lderate both mapped to the L state. The δthrottle observable provided evidence to distinguish
them, but thehmm’s posterior was expressed over L as a single state—the policy had to infer the
sub-mode from δthrottle directly rather than from a clean belief dimension. In v2, the posterior
over Lharvest is a separate number from the posterior over Lderate. The trap detection condition
becomes simply:
trap condition =P(L harvest)> θ trap ∧z aero = 1∧in activation zone (6)
This is directly actionable without post-hoc correction.
Proposition 1.The counter-harvest trap is not detectable by a single-observable threshold policy
on∆v trap alone.
Proof sketch. A car running ers = H without Active Aero produces ∆ vtrap ≈ +4 km/h. A car
in Lharvest with Active Aero in an activation zone produces ∆ vtrap ≈ −2 + 4 = +2 km/h. A car
in Lderate with Active Aero produces similarly ∆ vtrap ≈ +2 km/h. All three distributions overlap
under the emission model. No scalar threshold on ∆ vtrap can reliably separate them. The joint
signal (∆vtrap, zaero, δthrottle) provides separation: zaero = 1 with ∆ vtrap ∈ [0, +3] km/h andlow
δthrottle (< 0.15) identifies Lharvest with probability ≥ 0.85 under the emission model. The same
(∆vtrap, zaero) signature withhigh δthrottle (> 0.35) identifies Lderate—a genuine opportunity, not
a trap.
Circuit-dependent trap distinguishability.At low-regen circuits (Melbourne, recharge
ratio 1.0), super-clipping is mandatory for ∼16 s per lap, making Lderate the ambient state of most
cars on the grid. The zaero = 1 with depressed ∆ vtrap combination is therefore less diagnostic.
The rolling 5-lap baseline provides a partial rescue—a car in Lharvest will still produce positive
∆vtrap relative to the super-clipping field—but the margin narrows. The testable prediction is
that trap-detection recall at Melbourne will be lower than the 96.3% synthetic baseline and will
improve at higher-regen circuits.
4 Emission Model
4.1 Conditional Independence: A Tractable Baseline
We adopt conditional independence as a principled tractable baseline:
P(o t |x t, zzone) =
6Y
i=1
P(o t,i |x t, zzone) (7)
∆vtrap and ∆tsector are mechanically coupled: deploying moreerssimultaneously increases
speed and decreases sector time. Treating them as conditionally independent double-counts this
correlated evidence on every belief update, producing systematically over-confident posteriors.
The ECE figures reported in Section 7 are measured on synthetic data where the independence
assumption holds by construction—they are lower bounds on real-data calibration error. Tem-
perature scaling [Guo et al., 2017] is available as a post-hoc calibration step after Melbourne
data is available.
4.2 Observable Distributions
Observables 1–4 are modelled as Gaussian, observable 5 as Bernoulli, and observable 6 as a
truncated Gaussian on [0,1].

The signal separation between Lharvest and Lderate via δthrottle is |0.55 − 0.08| = 0 .47, more
than twice the combined standard deviation ( σ≈ 0.18). This separation—identified in v1.5 as
motivating a sixth observable—is the quantitative justification for elevating it to a state-level
distinction in v2.
Circuit-dependent prior for Lderate at Melbourne.At Melbourne (recharge ratio 1.0),
the estimated fraction of L laps that terminate in mandatory super-clipping is 0.40, giving a
blended prior mean of 0 .6 × 0.08 + 0.4 × 0.55 = 0.268. In v2 this blended prior is eliminated: the
HMM maintains separate posteriors over Lharvest and Lderate, and Baum-Welch will estimate
the circuit-specific transition rates between them directly from Race 1 telemetry.
4.3 Emission Signal Strength: Audit Results
erslevel is strongly identifiable: |µH −µ Lharvest| = 6.0 km/h in ∆vtrap and 18 m in ∆bbrake, both
substantially larger than the emission noise.
Lharvest vs. Lderate is identifiable via δthrottle: separation of 0.47, more than twice the combined
σ. This is the primary motivation for the v2 state-level split.
Tyre degradation signal is concentrated in the cliff state: ∆ tsector ≈ +0.8 s and ∆bbrake ≈
+16 m produce step changes the 5-lap baseline cannot absorb.
Override Mode status is not directly distinguishable from emissions in the non-active state
(differences < 0.5 km/h in ∆ vtrap). The Override activation event is strongly identifiable
(∆vtrap ≈+7 km/h, ∆t sector ≈ −0.65 s).
4.4 Observation Discretisation
Observations are discretised to form a finite joint observation space as specified in Appendix A:
∆vtrap (8 bins), ∆tsector (7 bins), ∆bbrake (5 bins), σ2
speed (5 bins), zaero (2 bins), δthrottle (6 bins).
Combined space: 8×7×5×5×2×6 = 16,800 bins.
The emission matrix E∈R 40×16800 is computed analytically by integrating the Gaussian,
Bernoulli, and truncated-Gaussian distributions over bin boundaries, conditioning on each of the
40 hidden states. Two matrices are maintained: Enormal (outside activation zones) and Ezone
(inside activation zones, with ∆v trap shifted by +4.0 km/h andz aero non-zero).
8
5 Inference Architecture
5.1 Layer 1: The HMM Belief Update
Thehmmhas 40 hidden states, emission matrix E∈R 40×16800, transition matrix T∈R 40×40,
and initial distributionπ∈∆ 40.
Transition model.The transition probability Tij = P (xt[+1] = j|x t = i) factors over the
three components under conditional independence:
Tij =P(e ′ |e, a)·P(m ′ |m)·P(τ ′ |τ) (13)
Theerstransition is marginalised over the rival’s action with estimatedP(burn):
P(e ′ |e) =p burn ·T burn
ee′ + (1−p burn)·T harvest
ee′ (14)
The Lharvest and Lderate sub-modes have different transition dynamics (Appendix B): a car
in Lharvest can transition to M or H under burn (it has reserve); a car in Lderate requires at
least one sector of managed throttle to recover to M, and cannot transition directly to H. This
asymmetry is strategically critical: it distinguishes a dangerous rival from a vulnerable one.
The Override Mode transition is proximity-conditioned. P (m′ = available|m = spent) =
P (gap< 1 s), which is partially observable from live timing data. The tyre transition is
monotone-absorbing. Full transition matrices are given in Appendix B.
Belief update.
αt(j) =P(o t |j)·

i
αt−1(i)·T ij (15)
Normalised to giveb t. Computational complexity:O(N 2) =O(1600) per sector.
Two-phase training.Phase 1 (pre-Melbourne): E is set analytically; T from physics-derived
transition parameters; π concentrates on ( e = H, m = available, τ = new). Phase 2 (post-
Melbourne): Baum-Welch EM [Baum et al., 1970] updatesEandTfrom real race sequences.
Alternating update schedule.After each race weekend: Phase A—freezedqnweights, run
Baum-Welch on new race data to update thehmm. Phase B—freezehmm, clear thedqnreplay
buffer, generate fresh synthetic experience from the updatedhmm, retraindqn.
5.2 Layer 2: The POMDP Policy
Input vector (66 dimensions).
Network architecture.
Input(66)→Dense(256,ReLU)→Dense(256,ReLU)→Dense(128,ReLU)→Dense(2)
Training.Double DQN [van Hasselt et al., 2016] with experience replay (buffer capacity
50,000; Huber loss; gradient clipping at 10). ε-greedy exploration decays from 1.0 to 0.05 over
synthetic pre-training.
Shaping reward.During synthetic pre-training only:R shaped =R+λ·Φ,λ= 0.3, where
Φ = +0.10·1[MAP(bt) =x ∗
t ]−0.20·1[trap condition∧a=burn]+0.05·1[gap ahead∈ {close,threat}∧e self ≥M]
(16)
Φ is zeroed during real-data fine-tuning.

On the information bottleneck.Thedqnreceives thehmmbelief state bt rather than raw
observables. In apomdp, the belief state is a sufficient statistic of the entire observation history.
In v2, the belief state now explicitly encodes P (Lharvest) and P (Lderate) as separate dimensions,
directly actionable by the policy. The δgap input provides a raw,hmm-independent signal for
closure rate.
6 Dataset
6.1 Data Source
Race telemetry is retrieved via the FastF1 Python library [Schaefer, 2024], which provides
access to the official FOM timing and telemetry feed at 10 Hz sampling. The car data endpoint
provides per-car speed, throttle, and braking data at sector resolution.
6.2 Observable Derivation
All six observables are computed as deviations from a per-driver rolling 5-lap baseline.
δthrottle derivation.For each sector, the fraction of straight-line telemetry samples in which
throttle ≥ 98% and speed is simultaneously below the driver’s 5-lap rolling speed baseline is
computed from the FastF1 car data Throttle channel at 10 Hz. If the Throttle channel is absent
for a given sector, δthrottle defaults to the circuit-appropriate prior mean for the inferred ERS
state.
Fuel exclusion.At ∼1.5 kg/lap over a 58-lap race, fuel burn produces a monotonic pace
improvement of approximately 0.03 s/lap. This per-lap drift falls within the στ = 0.15 s emission
noise; cumulative drift over the 5-lap baseline window (5 × 0.03 = 0.15 s) is absorbed by the
rolling baseline itself.
Full derivation pipelines for ∆b brake,σ 2
speed, andz aero are specified in Appendix D.
10
6.3 Dataset Statistics
Race coverage statistics are reported in subsequent work. All synthetic experiments use 20
simulated races at 174 sectors each (3,480 total sector observations).
7 Closed-Loop Synthetic Validation
7.1 Setup
This section reports a closed-loop evaluation: thehmmis tested on data generated by the same
parametric model that defines it. This is deliberately circular. It verifies that the components
work together as designed, but does not constitute empirical validation. Performance here is
therefore an upper bound on real-data performance, not an estimate of it. Empirical validation
begins with Race 1 data on 8 March 2026.
The generative model, strategy profiles, and observation noise specification are documented
in Appendix E. In brief: 20 synthetic races are generated (5 per strategy profile: aggressive,
conservative, trap-setter, balanced) using the physics-derived transition matrices with i.i.d.
Gaussian noise added to each continuous observable.
Baselines.
•B1—Deterministic Threshold: burn iff gap ahead∈ {close,threat}ANDe self ≥M.
•B2—Observable-Only Threshold: burn iff B1 conditions AND ∆v trap <0.
•B3—Oracle:pomdppolicy withb t replaced by the true hidden statex t (one-hot).
•B4—Full System: the proposedhmm+dqnpolicy.
7.2 HMM Inference Accuracy (Synthetic)
Table 4: HMM inference accuracy on synthetic races (pre-calibration, v2 with 40 states and
δthrottle). Random baselines: top-1 = 2.5%, ERS-level = 25.0% (4-class), MOM = 50.0%, tyre =
20.0%, harvest/derate = 50.0%.
Metric HMM Random Notes
Top-1 state accuracy 49.1% 2.5% Full 40-state identification
ERS level accuracy 96.8% 25.0% 4-class; primary inference target
Lharvest vs.L derate 89.4% 50.0% Key v2 capability
Override status accuracy 61.2% 50.0% Proximity-conditioned
Tyre cliff detection 91.3% 20.0% Step-change signal
Trap detection recall 96.3% — 117 trap sectors; 3.7% miss rate
ECE (calibration error) 0.006 — Lower is better; synthetic lower
bound
Gap to oracle (ERS level) 95.7% —
The 96.8% ERS-level accuracy (4-class, random baseline 25%) confirms strong emission signal
from ∆ vtrap, ∆ bbrake, and δthrottle. The improvement over v1.5 (92.3% with 3-class, random
baseline 33.3%) must be interpreted carefully: the random baselines differ (25% vs. 33.3%)
because the state space is larger. The gap-to-oracle metric of 95.7% provides a more comparable
measure of model quality across versions (v1.5: 88.0%, v1: same).
The new Lharvest vs. Lderate accuracy of 89.4%—not expressible in v1 or v1.5—is the headline
result of v2. It confirms that δthrottle provides sufficient discriminating power to support a
11
separate state for each sub-mode. The 10.6% error rate concentrates in Melbourne-analogue
circuits with high mandatory super-clipping, where the δthrottle baseline shifts upward for all
cars, narrowing the separation margin.
Trap detection recall of 96.3% (vs. 95.7% in v1.5) reflects the cleaner Lharvest posterior: false
trap activations caused by Lderate cars (the dominant error source in v1.5) are substantially
reduced.

7.4 Active Aero Threshold Sensitivity
Table 6: Trap recall and false positive rate vs. Active Aero detection threshold.
Threshold (km/h) Trap Recall False Positive Rate
1.0 97.9% 34.2%
1.5 95.1% 23.1%
2.0 91.4% 13.7%
2.5 85.2% 7.6%
3.0 75.3% 3.9%
3.5 63.1% 1.8%
The current 2.0 km/h threshold sits at the inflection point of the recall–FPR tradeoff. In
v2, false zaero detections produce a shifted posterior over Lharvest vs. Lderate—which can be
corrected on subsequent sectors—rather than directly triggering an action. The false positive
rate at the 2.0 km/h threshold improves from 15.3% (v1.5) to 13.7% (v2), attributable to the
cleaner posterior separation betweenLsub-modes.
7.5 HMM Calibration on Real Data
Baum-Welch calibration on 2026 race telemetry is reported in subsequent work.
8 Discussion
What the system does well.ERS state inference from ∆ vtrap and ∆bbrake is robust. Counter-
harvest trap detection is the clearest strength of the full system over observable-only baselines.
The v2 advance is the Lharvest posterior: where v1.5 required post-hoc correction to avoid false
trap activations fromL derate cars, v2 provides the distinction directly in the belief state.
12
The stationary opponent assumption.The most important limitation is structural. We
model rivals as stationary processes that do not adapt their strategy based on being observed.
Thepomdppolicy trained here is the correct baseline—the floor, not the ceiling, of performance
under adversarial conditions. Kleisarchaki [2026b] introduces the game-theoretic layer: the pit
wall strategy problem is formalised as a Keynesian beauty contest over joint belief states, and
the counter-harvest trap is characterised as an equilibrium strategy in the resulting partially
observable stochastic game.
Boost Mode exclusion.The 2026 regulations include two driver-controlled deployment
tools: proximity-constrained Override Mode and unconstrained Boost Mode. The present model
includes Override Mode but excludes Boost Mode as an explicit latent dimension. This exclusion
is deliberate rather than inadvertent. In the current observation design, the principal emissions
are tuned to distinguish latent energy-management states, especially deliberate harvesting versus
derating. By contrast, unconstrained Boost usage is expected to be identifiable primarily through
additional non-∆ vtrap observables, such as finer sector-level pace variation and non-straight
deployment signatures, which are outside the present emission architecture. Adding Boost
Mode as a further hidden dimension without those observation channels would introduce latent
distinctions that are not reliably identifiable from the current data model. We therefore treat
the Boost/harvest interaction as a separate inference problem and reserve its formalisation for
subsequent work.
Calibration.The conditional independence assumption produces over-confident beliefs. ECE =
0.006 on v2 synthetic data is a lower bound on real-data calibration error. Post-Baum-Welch
calibration on real data will partially improve this, but will not fully correct for the structural
violation between ∆ vtrap, ∆ tsector, and ∆ bbrake. A structural correction—replacing the con-
ditional independence assumption with bivariate Gaussian emission anders-state-dependent
correlations between ∆vtrap and ∆tsector—is introduced in Kleisarchaki [2026b] and addresses
the over-confidence at its source rather than correcting it post-hoc. Temperature scaling [Guo
et al., 2017] remains available as an additional post-hoc calibration step.
Data regime.At∼560 effective parameters and a limited dataset after one race, the Baum-
Welch estimates are Dirichlet-regularised guesses. The model should be treated as empirically
validated only from Race 4 onwards.
Transition matrix sector averaging.The global T burn and T harvest matrices are population
averages across track geometry. Circuit-conditioned transition matrices are the correct fix and
are deferred to Kleisarchaki [2026b].
Override Mode prior.The prior P (gap< 1 s) ≈ 0.25 governs Override Mode recovery when
live timing data is incomplete. The Melbourne pipeline conditions Pearn on the rival’s observed
gap to the car immediately ahead of them from the FOM live timing feed, reducing the residual
dependence on the 0.25 scalar prior.
Forward pointer to Kleisarchaki [2026b].The Lharvest/Lderate distinction is strategically
meaningful specifically because rivals reason about being observed—the core topic of Kleisarchaki
[2026b]. A rational trap-setter operates in Lharvest, not Lderate. The v2 belief state, by providing
P (Lharvest) as a separate dimension, gives the game-theoretic layer of Kleisarchaki [2026b] a
cleaner input.
13
9 Conclusion
We have presented a tractable two-layer framework for opponent state inference and decision-
making in 2026 Formula 1 energy strategy. The central advance of v2 is the decomposition of
ERS=Low into two strategically distinct states: Lharvest (deliberate conservation, hidden reserve
building, the trap condition) and Lderate (SOC ceiling, physical depletion, a genuine attack
opportunity). This decomposition, motivated by the δthrottle signal added in v1.5, is elevated
in v2 from a mixed emission to a full state-level distinction. The result is a 40-statehmmthat
provides directly actionable belief dimensions to thedqnpolicy, and a 96.3% trap detection
recall on synthetic data with a false positive rate substantially reduced from v1.5.
The stationary opponent assumption made here is precisely what Kleisarchaki [2026b] breaks.
A tractable approximate solution via Partially Observable Monte Carlo Tree Search with bounded
rationality is the subject of forthcoming work.

D FastF1 Observable Derivation Pipeline
Brake point delta.For each sector, we identify the track distance at which the car’s speed
begins monotonically decreasing from the sector’s speed maximum, using the 10 Hz speed trace.
A 3-sample Gaussian smoothing is applied before the monotone-descent detection to remove
telemetry noise.
Speed variance detrended.The within-sector speed trace is linearly detrended by fitting
and subtracting a first-order polynomial. The variance of the detrended residual is computed as
σ2
speed.
16
Active Aero detection.In designated activation zones, Active Aero deployment is inferred
from the speed residual after removing theers-explained component. A positive residual above
2.0 km/h is classified asz aero = 1.
Super-clipping duration ( δthrottle).For each sector, the fraction of straight-line telemetry
samples in which throttle ≥ 98% and speed is simultaneously below the driver’s 5-lap rolling
speed baseline is computed from the FastF1 car data Throttle channel at 10 Hz. If the Throttle
channel is absent, δthrottle defaults to the circuit-appropriate prior mean for the inferred ERS
state.

E.2 Observation Noise Model
Synthetic observations are generated from the emission parameters (Section 4) with i.i.d. Gaussian

noise) (18)

(truncation at 0). δthrottle is generated from a truncated Gaussian on [0 , 1] with the parameters
